methodological_rigor.justification: Retrospective case series from MSK (n=26 MSS CRC patients) who acquired high tumor mutational burden (TMB) and subsequently responded to immune checkpoint blockade. Patient identification through comprehensive genomic profiling is systematic and the molecular criteria for acquired TMB are clearly defined. The study appropriately acknowledges its retrospective, single-institution design as a major limitation. Multivariable analyses are limited given the small sample size; clinical outcomes (ORR, PFS, OS) are descriptively reported. The rarity of this phenomenon (MSS CRC responding to ICB) and systematic molecular characterization add methodological value despite design limitations.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: MSS colorectal cancer is broadly resistant to immune checkpoint blockade, making this case series of ICB responders with acquired TMB clinically significant. Identifying mechanisms by which MSS CRC can acquire ICB sensitivity (through mutagenic POLE/POLD1 mutations, mismatch repair alterations, or treatment-induced mutagenesis) has direct clinical implications for patient selection and treatment sequencing. These findings potentially establish a biomarker pathway for ICB use in MSS CRC, a large unmet-need population. LoE is 4 (retrospective case series) but clinical impact of identifying actionable mechanisms is high.

reporting_quality.justification: STROBE-adjacent reporting with patient selection flowchart, baseline characteristics, and genomic profiling methodology. The molecular characterization (TMB thresholds, mutation signatures, identified driver mutations for acquired TMB) is well-described. Clinical outcomes are reported with confidence intervals where feasible. STROBE checklist is not formally cited; some items regarding loss to follow-up and confounding adjustment are incompletely addressed given the small sample. Genomic data are referenced to MSK-IMPACT database with partial availability.

novelty_literature.justification: Acquired ICB sensitivity through treatment-associated mutagenesis in MSS CRC is a novel mechanism with significant clinical implications. While individual case reports of MSS CRC responding to ICB have been published, this systematic series with molecular characterization of the acquired TMB mechanism and correlation with ICB response represents a meaningful contribution. The characterization of specific mutagenic processes (APOBEC, alkylating agent signatures) driving acquired TMB fills a documented gap in understanding immunotherapy sensitivity evolution in colorectal cancer.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is clearly written with effective integration of genomic and clinical data. Oncoprints and mutation signature analyses are presented effectively alongside clinical outcome data. The narrative logically builds from molecular characterization to clinical implications. The discussion appropriately contextualizes acquired TMB within the broader landscape of MSS CRC ICB trials and addresses alternative explanations. Some limitations (retrospective design, single center, small sample) are acknowledged but could be more prominently discussed.

key_strengths: First systematic series characterizing acquired high TMB as a mechanism of ICB sensitivity in MSS colorectal cancer, addressing a critical unmet need in a historically ICB-resistant tumor type
Comprehensive molecular characterization of mutagenic processes (APOBEC, alkylating agent signatures, POLE/POLD1 mutations) driving acquired TMB provides mechanistic insight for patient selection
Clinical correlation between acquired TMB and ICB response in n=26 systematically identified patients provides proof-of-concept for a novel biomarker-treatment strategy
key_concerns: Small sample size (n=26) limits statistical power for clinical outcome analyses; confidence intervals for ORR and survival endpoints are very wide
Retrospective, single-institution design subject to referral bias and treatment heterogeneity; all patients from MSK with access to comprehensive genomic profiling
Causal attribution of ICB response to acquired TMB vs. other concurrent genomic or microenvironmental changes is not established
chief_reviewer.rationale: This systematic case series identifies acquired TMB as a novel mechanism of ICB sensitivity in MSS CRC — a finding with substantial clinical implications that justifies Tier 2 publication; the retrospective design and small sample are inherent to this rare molecular phenotype and are appropriately acknowledged.
